stem: In a reported study of **656 patients** undergoing aortic surgery with **deep hypothermic circulatory arrest (DHCA)**, how did stroke and mortality relate to the duration of circulatory arrest?

choices.text: Stroke increased after 25 minutes; mortality rose markedly after 40 minutes
Stroke increased after 65 minutes; mortality rose markedly after 40 minutes
Stroke increased after 40 minutes; mortality rose markedly after 65 minutes
Stroke increased after 60 minutes; mortality rose markedly after 90 minutes
Stroke increased after 30 minutes; mortality rose markedly after 45 minutes

explanation.text: In that study of **656 patients** having aortic surgery with DHCA, **stroke** increased after ==40 minutes== of circulatory arrest, and the **mortality rate** increased markedly after ==65 minutes==.

explanation.caption: Arrest duration and outcome (656 patients, DHCA)
head: Outcome
Increased after

explanation.title: As arrest time lengthened (656-patient DHCA series)
Stroke threshold first
explanation.text: In this series the **neurologic** threshold (stroke, 40 min) came **before** the mortality threshold (65 min). These are the findings of one reported study, not universal limits; do not swap them.
found that occurrence of stroke increased after 40 minutes of circulatory arrest, and the mortality rate increased markedly after 65 minutes of circulatory arrest.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 30

choiceNotes.a: 25 minutes is the **RCP duration** beyond which transient neurologic deficit was reported to increase, not the arrest threshold for stroke; stroke rose after 40 min and mortality after 65 min.
choiceNotes.b: The thresholds are reversed: **stroke** increased after 40 min and **mortality** rose markedly after 65 min.
choiceNotes.d: 60 minutes is the HCA time beyond which RCP was suggested to be especially useful; in this series stroke rose after **40 min** and mortality after **65 min**.
choiceNotes.e: These are not the reported thresholds; stroke increased after **40 min** and mortality rose markedly after **65 min**.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A surgeon plans **retrograde cerebral perfusion (RCP)** during deep hypothermic circulatory arrest for aortic arch replacement. Which statement about RCP is supported by the reported experience?

choices.text: It maintains cerebral hypothermia by cooling the whole head
It accelerates the onset of acidosis in the ischemic brain
It allows liberal use because it lowers transient neurologic deficit
Its benefit is confined to arrest periods shorter than 30 minutes
It made branched arch grafts unnecessary in total arch replacement

explanation.text: RCP was clearly effective in **maintaining cerebral hypothermia**, giving ==continuous cooling of the whole head==, and in **preventing air** from reaching the terminal vessels of the brain.

children: Continuous cooling of the whole head
Prevents air reaching the terminal vessels of the brain
May **delay** acidosis in the ischemic brain
Lower mortality and stroke rates (479 patients)
May extend the safe HCA period, especially when HCA > 60 min
Higher prevalence of transient neurologic deficit (TND)

explanation.title: Technique
explanation.text: When RCP is applied during **total arch replacement**, the **arch-first technique using a branched arch graft** became a standard procedure.
RCP is not risk-free: the **higher prevalence of TND** indicated the need for caution against overly liberal use.
RCP was clearly effective in maintaining cerebral hypothermia, providing continuous cooling of the whole head, and preventing air from reaching the terminal vessels of the brain.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 30

choiceNotes.b: By washing out some metabolites, RCP may **delay** (not accelerate) the onset of acidosis in the ischemic brain.
choiceNotes.c: The **higher prevalence of TND** with RCP indicated the need for caution against overly liberal use.
choiceNotes.d: RCP was suggested to extend the safe HCA period, **especially when HCA times are longer than 60 minutes**.
choiceNotes.e: When RCP was applied during total arch replacement, the **arch-first technique using a branched arch graft** became a standard procedure.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: During total arch replacement, the team is concerned about **transient neurologic deficit (TND)**. Which statement about the duration of cerebral perfusion and TND is supported?

choices.text: TND increased only with RCP; ACP duration had no effect on it
TND increased only when RCP exceeded 60 minutes
TND decreased as RCP duration increased beyond 25 minutes
TND increased when RCP exceeded 25 minutes, and with longer ACP
TND was avoided by prolonging ACP instead of RCP

explanation.text: TND incidence increased when **RCP lasted longer than ==25 minutes==**, and **longer antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP)** increased TND incidence as well.

explanation.caption: Duration and TND
head: Method
Effect of longer duration on TND

explanation.title: Neither method is a free pass
explanation.text: Prolonging **either** RCP or ACP was linked to more TND; the higher prevalence of TND with RCP argued against overly liberal use.
Hagl and colleagues warned that the incidence of TND increased if the duration of RCP exceeded 25 minutes, and that longer antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP) increased TND incidence as well.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 30

choiceNotes.b: The reported threshold for RCP was **25 minutes**; 60 minutes is the HCA time beyond which RCP was suggested to be especially helpful.
choiceNotes.c: The direction is reversed: TND **increased** when RCP exceeded 25 minutes.
choiceNotes.e: Longer ACP **increased** TND incidence as well.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: In the development of cerebral protection for aortic arch surgery, the term **"cerebroplegia"** describes which method?

choices.text: Retrograde cerebral perfusion during deep hypothermic arrest
Cold antegrade cerebral perfusion
Unilateral antegrade perfusion with reduced flow under moderate hypothermia
Antegrade cerebral perfusion through a four-branched graft
Arch-first replacement using a branched arch graft

explanation.text: In 1989 the **"cerebroplegia"** method was described as ==cold antegrade cerebral perfusion (ACP)==.

explanation.caption: Cerebral protection methods named in the history of arch surgery
head: Method
Description
rows: Reduced cerebral blood flow under **moderate** hypothermia; 90% survival after arch replacement
Excellent results in arch aneurysm, no neurologic sequel, 3 early deaths in 32 patients
Maintains cerebral hypothermia; prevents air reaching terminal cerebral vessels
Branched arch graft; standard when **RCP** is applied in total arch replacement

explanation.text: Cerebroplegia is **antegrade** and **cold**; do not confuse it with **retrograde** cerebral perfusion (RCP).
In 1989, Bachet and colleagues described the “cerebroplegia” method as cold ACP.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 30

choiceNotes.a: RCP is a different method (retrograde); cerebroplegia was described as **cold ACP**.
choiceNotes.c: Unilateral ACP with reduced cerebral blood flow under moderate hypothermia was a separate revival of ACP, not cerebroplegia.
choiceNotes.d: ACP using a **four-branched graft** technique was a separate report; cerebroplegia is **cold ACP**.
choiceNotes.e: The arch-first technique with a branched arch graft became standard when **RCP** was applied during total arch replacement.

stem: A basic hypothesis underlying hypothermic circulatory arrest is that a **safe duration** of arrest exists. According to this hypothesis, which describes a safe period of circulatory arrest?

choices.text: Absence of functional derangement, even if structural changes are present
A duration directly proportional to the temperature during arrest
Absence of early derangements, regardless of late findings
A duration that is independent of the temperature during arrest
Absence of detectable functional or structural derangement, early or late

explanation.text: A safe period means ==no detectable functional **or** structural organ derangement==, in the **early or late** postoperative period.

items: There is a **safe duration** of circulatory arrest.
Its length is **inversely related** to the temperature of the organism during arrest (colder -> longer).
Safety is judged by **both function and structure**, **early and late** after operation.

explanation.title: Structure counts, even without symptoms
explanation.text: Structural derangements **without apparent functional correlates** are of concern, particularly in the **central nervous system**, because they imply a **loss of neurologic reserve** that may matter later in life.
A safe period of circulatory arrest is characterized by absence of detectable functional or structural organ derangements in the early or late postoperative period.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 30

choiceNotes.a: Structural derangements without apparent functional correlates are of concern (especially in the CNS) because they imply a **loss of neurologic reserve**.
choiceNotes.b: The safe duration is **inversely** related to temperature during arrest.
choiceNotes.c: A safe period requires absence of derangements in the **early or late** postoperative period.
choiceNotes.d: The safe duration is hypothesized to be **inversely related** to temperature, not independent of it.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: A patient is cooled for circulatory arrest using **CPB alone (core cooling)** rather than surface cooling. Compared with surface cooling, which temperature pattern is expected?

choices.text: Rectal temperature is substantially lower than nasopharyngeal temperature
Rectal-nasopharyngeal order reverses; regional differences are considerable
Internal organ temperatures differ from one another by less than 2°C
Regional temperature differences widen as the cooling period is prolonged
Any single measurement site reliably represents whole-body temperature

explanation.text: With **core cooling** the rectal-to-nasopharyngeal relationship is ==reversed== and **regional differences are considerable**; prolonging cooling lessens them.

explanation.title: Name your site
explanation.text: When core cooling is used wholly or in part, **the specific site of temperature measurement**, and the limits of interpreting it, must be noted.

During cooling by hypothermic perfusion with CPB (core cooling), the relationship of rectal to nasopharyngeal temperature is reversed, and regional differences in temperature are considerable, although they can be lessened by prolonging the period of cooling.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, pp. 30–31

choiceNotes.a: Rectal temperature substantially lower than nasopharyngeal is the pattern of **surface cooling**; with core cooling it is reversed.
choiceNotes.c: Organ temperatures differing by less than 2°C describes **surface cooling**; core cooling produces considerable regional differences.
choiceNotes.d: Prolonging the period of cooling **lessens** regional differences.
choiceNotes.e: With core cooling the **specific site** of measurement and the limits of interpretation must be noted, because regional differences are considerable.

stem: One hypothesis holds that the magnitude of reduction in oxygen consumption relates **directly** to the safe duration of circulatory arrest. Why would a close numeric relationship between the two over a wide temperature range be surprising?

choices.text: Oxygen consumption cannot be used as an index of metabolic activity
Oxygen consumption increases as body temperature falls
Other phenomena during arrest, such as no-reflow, cause damage
Oxygen consumption falls to zero once the body is below 20°C
Tissue oxygen stores sustain metabolism throughout the arrest period

explanation.text: The V̇O~2~-to-safe-time link is ==only a hypothesis==. Other phenomena occur during arrest, notably **regional vascular occlusion** in the brain (and probably all organs) leading to the **no-reflow phenomenon**.

steps.label: so
steps.text: Available **energy stores** maintain cell viability through the ischemic arrest

explanation.title: Why the link may break
explanation.text: **No-reflow** is an obstructive lesion of the microcirculation that prevents local reperfusion and leads to additional damage **after** the general circulation of blood has been reestablished.
It is only a hypothesis that a numeric relationship exists between V̇O~2~ and safe circulatory arrest time at any given temperature.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 32

choiceNotes.a: V̇O~2~ **is** considered a measure of metabolic activity; its decrease by hypothermia is an index of the reduction of metabolic activity.
choiceNotes.b: Energy requirements, reflected in part by V̇O~2~, are **reduced** during hypothermia.
choiceNotes.d: V̇O~2~ is **not reduced to near zero** even at temperatures close to 0°C.
choiceNotes.e: For all practical purposes, tissue and cellular **stores of oxygen do not exist**.

stem: During aortic arch surgery, the patient's nasopharyngeal temperature is held at **26°C**. By the expert consensus grading of hypothermia, this level is

choices.text: Mild hypothermia
Low-moderate hypothermia
Deep hypothermia
High-moderate hypothermia
Profound hypothermia

explanation.text: **26°C** falls in ==high-moderate hypothermia== (24.1°C–28.0°C).
**Moderate** hypothermia (20.1°C–28°C) is split in two at **24°C**: low-moderate below, high-moderate above.
moderate hypothermia ranges from 20.1°C to 28°C (low-moderate hypothermia 20.1°C–24°C, high-moderate hypothermia 24.1°C–28.0°C)
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 31

stem: By the expert consensus grading of hypothermia, which temperature range defines **deep hypothermia**?

choices.text: 14°C or lower

explanation.text: **Deep** hypothermia is ==14.1°C to 20°C==; anything ≤ 14°C is **profound**.
**Deep** and **profound** are not synonyms: the boundary between them is **14°C**.
profound hypothermia is defined as ≤14°C, deep hypothermia as 14.1°C to 20°C
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 31

stem: During aortic arch surgery, brain temperature is estimated from surrogate sites rather than measured directly by jugular bulb temperature. Besides the nasopharynx and tympanic membrane, which site has the **best correlation** with jugular bulb temperature?

choices.text: Rectum
Urinary bladder
CPB arterial outlet
Midesophagus
Extremity skin

explanation.text: The **nasopharynx**, **tympanic membrane**, and ==arterial blood outlet of CPB== have the best correlation with **jugular bulb** temperature.

explanation.caption: Temperature sites during arch surgery
head: Site
What the source says
rows: **Best correlation** with jugular bulb temperature; many use them as **brain** temperature, even during circulatory arrest
**Best correlation** with jugular bulb temperature; some studies recommend it as a surrogate for cerebral temperature during CPB

explanation.text: Accurate brain temperature is **essential for cerebral protection** in arch surgery, and surrogate sites are used instead of directly measuring brain temperature by jugular bulb temperature.
Temperatures measured in the nasopharynx, tympanic membrane, and the arterial blood outlet of CPB have the best correlation with jugular bulb temperature.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 31

choiceNotes.a: Rectal temperature is used as a **systemic core** temperature; the sites with the best correlation with jugular bulb temperature are the nasopharynx, tympanic membrane and **CPB arterial outlet**.
choiceNotes.b: Bladder temperature is used as a **systemic core** temperature; the sites with the best correlation with jugular bulb temperature are the nasopharynx, tympanic membrane and **CPB arterial outlet**.
choiceNotes.d: The midesophagus is one of the varied sites used to estimate temperature, but it is not among the sites with the best correlation with jugular bulb temperature (nasopharynx, tympanic membrane, **CPB arterial outlet**).
choiceNotes.e: Extremity skin is one of the varied sites used to estimate temperature, but it is not among the sites with the best correlation with jugular bulb temperature; with surface cooling, skin becomes cooler than inner organs.

stem: Oxygen consumption (V̇O~2~) is used as an index of the reduction in metabolic activity produced by hypothermia in the anesthetized subject. Why is this use reasonable?

choices.text: Oxygen consumption is linearly related to body temperature
Shivering keeps oxygen consumption proportional to heat loss
Oxygen consumption falls to near zero at temperatures near 0°C
Q~10~ values are identical in every tissue
Tissues and cells have practically no oxygen stores

explanation.text: Because ==tissue and cellular oxygen stores do not exist== for practical purposes, the oxygen the body consumes mirrors its **metabolic needs**.

steps.label: so
steps.text: Body depends on the **circulation** to bring oxygen

steps.label: so
steps.text: Fall in V̇O~2~ = index of fall in **metabolic activity**

explanation.title: Condition
explanation.text: The index applies to the **anesthetized** subject in whom **shivering is prevented**.
Use of V̇O~2~ as such a marker is reasonable because, for all practical purposes, tissue and cellular stores of oxygen do not exist.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 31

choiceNotes.a: The relationship of V̇O~2~ to temperature is **not linear** (Box 2.1).
choiceNotes.b: The index applies to the anesthetized subject **in whom shivering is prevented**.
choiceNotes.c: V̇O~2~ is **not reduced to near zero** at temperatures close to 0°C.
choiceNotes.d: Q~10~ **differs from tissue to tissue** (on average about 2); the use of V̇O~2~ as a marker rests on the absence of tissue and cellular oxygen stores.

stem: Experimental data relating whole-body oxygen consumption to body temperature in surface-cooled animals were reanalyzed with several mathematical models. Which model best fits these data, and also the relation between temperature and **cerebral oxygen consumption during CPB in humans**?

choices.text: The Arrhenius equation
A linear equation
A hyperbolic equation
A log-log relation
The van't Hoff law

explanation.text: The ==van't Hoff law== best fits the combined surface-cooling data and is considered the **most appropriate model**; it also best fits **cerebral** oxygen consumption during CPB in humans.

explanation.caption: Models of oxygen consumption (Box 2.1)
head: Model
What it expresses
rows: Log of reaction rate **directly** related to temperature; rate rises **2–3 times per 10°C**
Log of rate inversely proportional to the reciprocal of **absolute** temperature; **S-shaped** curve with an asymptote at high temperatures
Also tested on the data; not the best fit

explanation.text: At physiologic temperatures, biochemical systems operate only on the **upswing** of the S-shaped Arrhenius curve, so, over a relatively small temperature range, the relation is expressed by the **van't Hoff law**.

explanation.title: Fig. 2.1
explanation.text: The van't Hoff regression of whole-body V̇O~2~ in surface-cooled dogs has a slope indicating a **Q~10~ of 2.7**.
The van’t Hoff law best fits this combined set of data (Fig. 2.1) and is considered the most appropriate model for this purpose.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 32

choiceNotes.a: The Arrhenius equation was one of the models used in the reanalysis, but the **van't Hoff law** fit best.
choiceNotes.b: A linear equation was one of the models used in the reanalysis, but the **van't Hoff law** fit best.
choiceNotes.c: The hyperbolic equation in Box 2.1 relates V̇O~2~ to **perfusion flow rate**, not to temperature.
choiceNotes.d: A log-log relation is listed among empirical relations that may describe actual data; it was not reported as the best fit here.

stem: Box 2.1 defines **Q~10~** so that when T~1~ − T~2~ is 10°C, Q~10~ is simply the ratio of the metabolic rates k~1~/k~2~. Applying this definition to a tissue with a Q~10~ of **2**, if its metabolic rate at 37°C is taken as 100%, its metabolic rate at **27°C** is

explanation.text: This is a direct application of the definition: for a 10°C difference, **Q~10~ = k~1~/k~2~**. With Q~10~ = 2, the rate at 27°C = rate at 37°C ÷ 2, so cooling 37°C -> 27°C ==halves== the rate: 100% ÷ 2 = **50%**.
**Q~10~** is the multiple by which the reaction rate changes per **10°C** change in temperature; by the van't Hoff law the rate increases **two to three times** for a 10°C rise.

explanation.title: Q~10~ values in the source
items: Tissue slices and isolated organs: about **2** on average (differs from tissue to tissue)

explanation.text: If T1 − T2 is 10°, then Q10 is simply the ratio of k1 to k2 (metabolic rates at each temperature).
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 31, Box 2.1

choiceNotes.a: 25% corresponds to a Q~10~ of **4** (100 ÷ 4); with Q~10~ = 2 a single 10°C fall gives 100 ÷ 2 = **50%**.
choiceNotes.c: 67% corresponds to a Q~10~ of about **1.5** (100 ÷ 1.5); with Q~10~ = 2 the rate at 27°C is 100 ÷ 2 = **50%**.
choiceNotes.d: 80% corresponds to a Q~10~ of **1.25** (100 ÷ 1.25); with Q~10~ = 2 the rate at 27°C is 100 ÷ 2 = **50%**.
choiceNotes.e: 20% corresponds to a Q~10~ of **5** (100 ÷ 5); with Q~10~ = 2 the rate at 27°C is 100 ÷ 2 = **50%**.

stem: Whole-body oxygen consumption measured before and after **heating** gives a Q~10~ of about 1.9. If **cooling** yields a Q~10~ clearly greater than 1.9, what may this indicate?

choices.text: Tissue oxygen stores are being used up during cooling
True tissue oxygen requirement rises as the body cools
Vasodilatation has improved oxygen access to the tissues
Oxygen delivery is limited by an inadequate flow rate
Metabolic activity has ceased at the lower temperature

explanation.text: A Q~10~ **greater than 1.9** with cooling may mean the fall in V̇O~2~ is partly ==supply-limited==: oxygen delivery compromised by an **inadequate flow rate**.

explanation.title: Why heating shows the true requirement

steps.label: ensures
steps.text: Access of oxygen to the tissues

steps.label: so
steps.text: Q~10~ about **1.9** probably = **true tissue oxygen requirement**

explanation.title: Whole-body data may mislead
explanation.text: Only areas whose **microcirculation is still perfused** can consume oxygen, so whole-body data could **underestimate true oxygen demand**; part of the fall may come from shutting down the microcirculation or from arteriovenous shunting.
A Q10 greater than 1.9 associated with cooling may indicate that oxygen delivery has been compromised by inadequate flow rate.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 32

choiceNotes.a: Tissue and cellular oxygen stores are **trivial**, so there are essentially no stores to use up.
choiceNotes.b: Energy requirements are **reduced** by hypothermia; a high Q~10~ suggests limited delivery, not a higher requirement.
choiceNotes.c: Vasodilatation is the effect of **heating**, which ensures oxygen access and gives the lower Q~10~ of about 1.9.
choiceNotes.e: V̇O~2~ is **not reduced to near zero** even at temperatures close to 0°C; metabolic activity continues.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass
source.loc: p. 32, Oxygen Consumption During Hypothermia in Tissue Slices and Isolated Organs

stem: In experimental studies, rats cooled by immersion to 18°C had a **33% lower oxygen consumption** than expected from tissue slice respiration at that temperature. Which explanation was proposed for this discrepancy?

choices.text: Arteriovenous shunting or regional perfusion shutdown
Inhomogeneities in whole-body temperature during immersion
Known changes in Q~10~ exhibited by some tissues
Catecholamine release increasing whole-body oxygen consumption
Oxygen supplied from tissue and cellular stores

explanation.text: The precise mechanism is unknown; it could be ==arteriovenous shunting== or **shutting down perfusion in some body areas**, which microvascular physiologists call a **decrease in effective capillary density**.

branches.text: Changes in red cell geometry and compliance

explanation.title: Already excluded
explanation.text: The discrepancy was **not** accounted for by inhomogeneities in whole-body temperature or by known changes in Q~10~ in some tissues.
It could be due to arteriovenous shunting or shutting down perfusion in some body areas. Microvascular physiologists have referred to the latter as a decrease in effective capillary density.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 32

choiceNotes.b: The discrepancy was **not** accounted for by inhomogeneities in whole-body temperature.
choiceNotes.c: The discrepancy was **not** accounted for by known changes in Q~10~ exhibited by some tissues.
choiceNotes.d: Catecholamine release is cited as a cause of **increased** V̇O~2~ during whole-body perfusion; it cannot explain a lower V̇O~2~.
choiceNotes.e: Tissue and cellular oxygen stores are **trivial**.

stem: Some studies of tissue slices and isolated perfused organs show a **greater** relative reduction in oxygen consumption with hypothermia than is seen in the body as a whole. Which is a proposed reason?

choices.text: Optimal conditions for tissue respiration in the slice studies
Absence of species differences in tissue respiration
Oxygen stores within intact tissues sustaining consumption
Catecholamine-driven rise in whole-body oxygen consumption
Uniform Q~10~ values across all tissues and organs

explanation.text: During **whole-body perfusion**, V̇O~2~ may be ==increased==, for example by **catecholamine release**, so the whole body shows a smaller relative reduction than isolated tissue (Table 2.1).

items: **Suboptimal** conditions for tissue respiration in the tissue slice studies
**Increased V̇O~2~ during whole-body perfusion**, for example from **catecholamine release**

explanation.title: Still reduced
explanation.text: Tissue slice studies confirm that oxygen consumption **is** reduced by hypothermia; Q~10~ differs from tissue to tissue, averaging about **2**.

This may be related to known species differences in tissue respiration, suboptimal conditions for tissue respiration in the studies with tissue slices, or increased V̇O~2~ during whole-body perfusion caused, for example, by catecholamine release.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 32

choiceNotes.a: Conditions for tissue respiration in the slice studies were proposed to be **suboptimal**.
choiceNotes.b: Known **species differences** in tissue respiration are one of the proposed reasons.
choiceNotes.c: Tissue and cellular oxygen stores are **trivial**.
choiceNotes.e: Q~10~ **differs from tissue to tissue**, averaging about 2.

stem: A patient undergoes circulatory arrest after deep cooling. Which statement about metabolism and temperature **during the arrest period** is supported?

choices.text: Organs continue to cool passively throughout the arrest period
Oxygen consumption is not reduced to near zero, even close to 0°C
Brain temperature rises only because of the brain-to-room gradient
Metabolic activity ceases once the brain reaches 1°C to 2°C
Safe arrest time becomes unlimited once deep hypothermia is reached

explanation.text: V̇O~2~ is ==not reduced to near zero== at temperatures close to 0°C, so metabolism continues and the **time limits of safe circulatory arrest must be finite**.

steps.text: V̇O~2~ not near zero, even close to 0°C

explanation.title: Experimental brain rewarming
explanation.text: In dog brains cooled to **1°C to 2°C**, temperature **rose** during 30 minutes of circulatory arrest, partly from the **gradient between brain and room temperature** and partly from **continuing brain metabolism**.
Metabolic activity is therefore continuing, and the time limits of safe circulatory arrest must be finite.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 32

choiceNotes.a: Continuing metabolic activity causes a tendency for organs and systems to **rewarm** during the arrest period.
choiceNotes.c: The rise was related **in part** to the brain-to-room gradient and **in part** to continuing metabolic activity in the brain.
choiceNotes.d: In dog brains cooled to 1°C to 2°C, temperature rose during arrest partly from **continuing metabolic activity**.
choiceNotes.e: Because metabolic activity continues, the time limits of safe circulatory arrest **must be finite**.

stem: The **no-reflow phenomenon** could theoretically damage the brain after hypothermic circulatory arrest. What did experimental studies show about its cause and prevention?

choices.text: It results from severe hypoxia or anoxia, and hypothermia to 20°C prevented it
It results from circulatory arrest per se, and hypothermia did not prevent it
It results from severe hypoxia or anoxia, and only normothermia prevented it
It results from circulatory arrest per se, and hypothermia to 20°C prevented it
It results from reperfusion alone, independent of any oxygen deprivation

explanation.text: No-reflow develops from ==severe hypoxia or anoxia==, **not** from circulatory arrest per se, and **hypothermia to 20°C** prevented it after 90 minutes of anoxia.

steps.text: Regional vascular occlusion (brain, probably all organs)

steps.label: leads to
steps.text: Additional damage **after** the general circulation is reestablished

explanation.text: In the experiment, anoxia was produced by **continuing perfusion at an arterial Pao~2~ of about 10 mmHg** for 90 minutes; at **20°C** the no-reflow phenomenon did not follow.
Do not blame the **arrest itself**: the trigger is **severe hypoxia or anoxia**.
Norwood and colleagues have shown experimentally that this phenomenon develops as a result of severe hypoxia or anoxia, not because of circulatory arrest per se.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 32

choiceNotes.b: No-reflow develops from severe hypoxia or anoxia, **not because of circulatory arrest per se**, and hypothermia to 20°C **prevented** it.
choiceNotes.c: **Hypothermia to 20°C** prevented no-reflow after 90 minutes of anoxia.
choiceNotes.d: The cause is severe hypoxia or anoxia, **not circulatory arrest per se**.
choiceNotes.e: No-reflow was shown to develop as a result of **severe hypoxia or anoxia**.

stem: No-reflow may represent, at least in part, **hypoxic endothelial cell injury**. In experimental studies, which response follows hypoxia and reoxygenation?

choices.text: Endothelin-1 release falls; hypothermia reverses the fall
Endothelin-1 nearly doubles; hypothermia augments the response
An anticoagulant response that prevents microthrombosis
Relaxing-factor release only; constricting factors unchanged
Endothelin-1 nearly doubles; hypothermia blunts the response

explanation.text: Hypoxia then reoxygenation causes an ==almost twofold increase in endothelin-1== release by endothelial cells; this response **can be blunted when ischemia is induced under hypothermia**.
**Endothelin-1** is described as the **most powerful vasoconstrictor** yet identified. Hypothermia may therefore **protect against hypoxic endothelial cell injury**.

explanation.center: Impaired perfusion after ischemia despite restored flow

explanation.text: In experimental studies, hypoxia followed by reoxygenation results in an almost twofold increase in release by endothelial cells of endothelin-1, the most powerful vasoconstrictor yet identified.
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 33

choiceNotes.a: Endothelin-1 release **increases** almost twofold after hypoxia and reoxygenation, and the response can be **blunted** when ischemia is induced under hypothermic conditions.
choiceNotes.b: The endothelin-1 response can be **blunted** (not augmented) when ischemia is induced under hypothermic conditions.
choiceNotes.c: Hypoxia may promote a **procoagulant** response in endothelial cells, which can result in intravascular microthrombosis.
choiceNotes.d: Hypoxic endothelial injury involves altered expression of **both** relaxing and constricting factors, with increased endothelin-1.

source.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass

stem: An infant is **surface cooled to 25°C** before circulatory arrest. Which change in the blood has been demonstrated during such cooling?

choices.text: Progressive hemodilution with an expanded plasma volume
Stable hematocrit with an unchanged plasma volume
Progressive hemoconcentration with a decreased plasma volume
Progressive hemoconcentration with an increased plasma volume
Hemodilution from interstitial fluid entering the vascular bed

explanation.text: Surface cooling of infants to 25°C causes ==progressive hemoconcentration== and **decreased plasma volume**.

branches.label: plasma
branches.text: **Sequestered** in portions of the vascular bed

explanation.text: The proposed shift is plasma moving **out of** the circulation (sequestered in parts of the vascular bed or leaking into the interstitium), not fluid entering it.
Chen and colleagues demonstrated progressive hemoconcentration and decreased plasma volume during surface cooling of infants to 25°C
explanation.ref: Chapter 2: Hypothermia, Circulatory Arrest, and Cardiopulmonary Bypass, p. 34

choiceNotes.a: Surface cooling produced **hemoconcentration** and a **decreased** plasma volume.
choiceNotes.d: Plasma volume **decreased**; that is what concentrates the blood.
choiceNotes.e: Plasma may **leak into** the interstitial fluid compartment (and be sequestered in the vascular bed), giving hemoconcentration rather than hemodilution.
